description: We are two second-year students at Kozybayev University: one studies robotics, the other data science and IT. We love physics, robotics and electronics, and we are always working on improving our skills. At NASA Space Apps we want to build something really cool by combining hardware and data. Our team is complete, and we are excited to take on the challenge together.
summary: Rice Rhythm uses NISAR L-band radar to track water on rice fields through the whole season. Flooded paddies emit 10–13% of human-made methane and rice uses 24–30% of the world's freshwater withdrawals. Water-saving practices such as direct-seeded rice (DSR) exist, and governments pay farmers to adopt them, but checking claims is slow. In Haryana, India, 69% of the claimed DSR area in 2024 was not confirmed by field inspection, and honest farmers waited about 9 months for payment. NISAR sees water through clouds and under the crop canopy. We built an open pipeline that reads NISAR GCOV data, turns each 300 m cell into a seasonal "rhythm" of radar backscatter, maps rice and flags fields with sudden changes. In Kyzylorda, Kazakhstan, 11 NISAR scenes revealed 453 rice cells; agreement with Sentinel-2 water detection was 72% (balanced accuracy). Goal: inspectors visit only the fields where radar disagrees with the claim.
details:
What it does: Rice Rhythm reads NISAR L2 GCOV (HH and HV, L-band) over a region, stacks all dates of one season and builds a time series for every 300×300 m cell. HH responds to water and soil, HV to vegetation. Rules on these series separate rice from other land and flag cells with sudden changes. Output: an interactive map (click a cell to see its season chart), charts, a before/after radar view.

Results (Zhalagash, Kyzylorda, track 078D, 19 Jun–29 Oct 2026): 5,056 cells analysed, 453 rice cells. One rice block showed a sharp change in late September, confirmed by a second independent NISAR track (150D). Validation against Sentinel-2 water index on ~3,000 cell-date pairs: 92% raw agreement, 72% balanced accuracy. A blind test in Arkansas (AmeriFlux sites) showed the rules need regional calibration.

Impact: an open, low-cost way to tell inspectors which fields to check first, for subsidy programmes such as Haryana's DSR incentive (₹4,000/acre). Scales to any rice region NISAR covers.

Creativity: each field is treated as a seasonal "rhythm" instead of a single image, using new L-band data that sees water under the canopy, where C-band and optical sensors struggle.

Tools: Python (asf_search, h5py, xarray, rasterio, pyproj, shapely, folium, matplotlib), NASA Earthdata, ASF DAAC, Microsoft Planetary Computer.

Limitations: 12-day revisit; no calibrated data before 17 June 2026; DSR vs transplanting not yet tested on labelled fields. Next step: Haryana in the 2027 season.

An AI coding assistant was used to help write code and edit text. The team chose the problem, region and data, made the analysis decisions and validated the results.
